test_title: PYST 71: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 29 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: A science teacher asks students to measure the current through a bulb using an ammeter. What precaution must the students follow?

options.text: Connect the ammeter without a battery
Connect the ammeter in series with correct polarity
Connect the ammeter with reversed polarity
Connect the ammeter in parallel with the bulb

solution:
The correct answer is __**Connect the ammeter in series with correct polarity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An **ammeter** is a measuring instrument used to measure the **electric current** in a circuit. To measure the current passing through a component like a **bulb**, the ammeter must be connected in **series** so that the entire current of the circuit flows through it.
 
• The **polarity** of the ammeter is a critical precaution; the **positive terminal** (usually marked **red** or with a **plus sign**) must be connected to the wire coming from the **positive terminal** of the **battery**, and the **negative terminal** (usually **black**) should be directed towards the **negative terminal**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• Connecting an ammeter without a **battery** or power source is futile because there is no **Electromotive Force (EMF)** to drive the flow of **electrons**, resulting in a zero reading. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• If an ammeter is connected with **reversed polarity**, the **pointer** in an analog meter will try to move in the opposite direction (below zero), which can cause **mechanical damage** to the needle or provide a negative reading on a **digital multimeter**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Connecting an ammeter in **parallel** with a load (like a bulb) is dangerous because ammeters have **very low internal resistance**. A parallel connection creates a **short circuit**, allowing a massive amount of current to flow through the ammeter, which can **burn the coil** or blow the **internal fuse**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ideal Ammeter Characteristics**:
 
 
• An **ideal ammeter** is defined as having **zero resistance**. This ensures that its inclusion in the circuit does not alter the total **resistance** and, consequently, does not change the **current** it is intended to measure.
 
• In practice, **real ammeters** have a very small but non-zero resistance, which causes a negligible **voltage drop** across them.
 
 
 
• **Galvanometer to Ammeter Conversion**:
 
 
• An ammeter is typically constructed by connecting a **low resistance** wire, known as a **Shunt**, in **parallel** with a sensitive **Galvanometer**.
 
• The **shunt resistance** allows the majority of the current to bypass the delicate galvanometer coil, enabling the measurement of **large currents** without damaging the instrument.
 
 
 
• **Units and History**:
 
 
• The unit of electric current is the **Ampere (A)**, which is one of the seven **SI base units**. It is defined as the flow of **one Coulomb** of charge per **second**.
 
• The instrument is named after the French physicist **André-Marie Ampère**, who made significant contributions to the study of **electromagnetism** in the **1820s**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Voltmeter**:
 
 
• Unlike an ammeter, a **voltmeter** is used to measure **potential difference** and is always connected in **parallel**.
 
• A voltmeter possesses **high resistance** to ensure it draws minimal current from the main circuit, whereas an ammeter requires **low resistance** to allow maximum current through it.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Safety Protocols**: Before turning on the power, always verify the **range** of the ammeter. If the current exceeds the **maximum scale deflection**, the device may be permanently damaged.
 
• **Types of Ammeters**: Modern science uses various types, including **Moving Coil Ammeters** (for DC), **Moving Iron Ammeters** (for both AC and DC), and **Digital Ammeters** which use **analog-to-digital converters (ADC)** for high precision.
 
• **Circuit symbols**: In a standard **circuit diagram**, an ammeter is represented by a **circle** with the letter **'A'** inside it, placed in the path of the current flow.
